title: Rapidly progressive dementia: probable sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease in a Yoruba Nigerian woman with rapidly progressive dementia: a case report
case_prompt:
A 68-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a 6-week history of progressive memory decline and behavioral changes. She became unable to perform her daily activities (cooking, bathing, managing funds), spoke out of context with irrational behavior, missed her way around the house, and had occasional visual hallucinations. There was no tremor, stiffness, head trauma, stroke, or known psychiatric history. Her older sister experienced progressive memory loss in her late 60s and died 5 years after symptom onset; details were unavailable. Medical history was notable for well-controlled hypertension; she did not drink alcohol or smoke.

On examination, she was conscious but oriented only to person. Immediate, short-term, and remote memory were severely impaired (MMSE score 2/30). Neurologic examination revealed quadriparesis (MRC grade 3), hypertonia, hyperreflexia, and an extensor plantar response in the right lower limb. Other systemic findings were unremarkable. An initial assessment of rapidly progressive dementia was made, with acute psychotic disorder considered.

Laboratory studies showed:
– White blood cell count 16,600/µL (neutrophils 96%), platelets 107,000/µL  
– Serum sodium 155 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L, urea 13.6 mmol/L  
– AST 103 IU/L, ALT 128 IU/L; other liver function tests within normal limits  
– Thyroid function tests (TSH, fT3, fT4) within normal ranges  
– HIV serology negative, blood and urine cultures negative  

The patient underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Thyroid dysfunction — “Other common causes of rapidly progressive dementia, such as thyroid dysfunction ... were excluded.”  
2. Hepatic encephalopathy — “Other common causes of rapidly progressive dementia, such as ... hepatic encephalopathy ... were excluded.”  
3. Cerebral infarction — “Other common causes of rapidly progressive dementia, such as ... cerebral infarction ... were excluded.”  
4. HIV infection — “Other common causes of rapidly progressive dementia, such as ... HIV were excluded.”  
5. Fatal familial insomnia — “A close differential is also fatal familial insomnia, in which ... insomnia, phobia, panic attacks, and hallucinations usually precede memory problems, unlike in CJD.”  
6. Probable sporadic CJD — “The patient was diagnosed with probable sporadic CJD because of the presentation of rapidly progressive dementia, ataxia, myoclonic jerks of the upper limbs, brain MRI findings (cortical ribbon sign ...), and typical EEG findings (periodic sharp and slow wave complexes).”
